title: Early practice doesn't look like the test
statement: Spend most of a course teaching and building knowledge rather than drilling the final test, keeping test-format practice to set points late in the sequence.
detail: The evaluation gauntlet in one course-plan program runs a marathon-rule probe on reading courses: early practice should mostly not look like the test but be vocabulary in context, monitoring prompts and knowledge work, with test-format practice concentrated late and timed conditions last (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/train-teacher/references/gauntlet-spec.md`). The reading-comprehension BrainLift in the same work holds that assessment format is not instruction format (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/teaching-reading-comprehension-brainlift.md`). The Grade 3 reading criteria require knowledge-building activity that looks nothing like the paragraph-plus-questions test (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/dimensions/D7-knowledge-first-curriculum.md`), and the practice-layer spec has format fluency taught as the operations each format demands of the text, never drilled (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/practice-layer-spec.md`). Timed conditions come last, and test-format practice is framed as practice, never as instruction.

evidence.quote: **Marathon-rule probe** (reading): does early practice look like the test? (It mostly shouldn't — vocabulary-in-context, monitoring prompts, knowledge work; test-format practice concentrated late, timed conditions last.)
Assessment format is not instruction format (the marathon rule), and acquisition mastery is not durable mastery — they need different instruments
